chief_complaint: Give a routine end-of-shift SBAR signout for a stable, recovering patient to the night covering resident

team_brief.title: Routine signout: stable post-op day 3 after total hip replacement
team_brief.patient: Mrs. Helen Barros, 71-year-old woman, post-op day 3 from an elective right total hip replacement
team_brief.location: Orthopedic ward, end of your day shift; you are handing over to the night covering resident
team_brief.situation: She is recovering well and there is no active problem, but the night team needs a clear, complete signout in case anything changes overnight.
background: Elective right total hip replacement three days ago; uncomplicated surgery and recovery so far.
Started on a standard post-operative anticoagulant for VTE prophylaxis and has been mobilizing with physiotherapy since day 1.
current_status: Afebrile, vitals stable, pain well controlled on oral analgesia.
Wound clean and dry; walking short distances with a frame today.
key_data: One watch item: her evening dose of the anticoagulant is due at 20:00 and has not yet been given.
Labs from this morning were unremarkable; no results are pending.
treatments: Oral analgesia, standard VTE prophylaxis anticoagulant, and physiotherapy-directed mobilization.
team_brief.your_request: Give a concise, structured SBAR signout so the night resident knows the plan and the one thing that still needs to happen tonight.
must_include: Who the patient is and why she is a routine, low-concern signout (Situation).
The surgery, day post-op, and course so far (Background).
Your assessment that she is stable with no active issues (Assessment).
The one specific action still needed overnight: giving the 20:00 anticoagulant dose (Recommendation).

kickoff_text: Hey, I'm on for nights. What have you got for me on the ortho list?
persona_override: You are Dr. Osei, the night covering resident receiving a routine end-of-shift signout. Mrs. Barros is post-op day 3 from an uncomplicated total hip replacement, stable, afebrile, mobilizing well, with one outstanding task: her 20:00 VTE prophylaxis dose has not yet been given. If the learner gives a clear, complete SBAR that names her as low-concern but still tells you the outstanding anticoagulant dose, acknowledge it warmly, confirm you will make sure the 20:00 dose is given, and ask if there is anything else. If the learner gives only a vague summary ('she's fine, nothing to worry about') and omits the specific outstanding dose, ask directly: 'Is there anything outstanding I need to action tonight, or any medications due?' so the learner experiences why even a routine handover needs a specific action item, not just reassurance. Stay friendly and unhurried throughout — this is not an urgent call.
learning_objectives: recognize that even a routine, low-concern patient needs a structured signout, not just a general reassurance
state who the patient is and why the case is low-concern (Situation)
summarize the relevant surgical and post-operative course concisely (Background)
give a clear assessment that the patient is currently stable
name the one specific outstanding action for the night team (Recommendation)
suggested_questions: This is Mrs. Barros, post-op day 3 from a hip replacement — she's stable, so this is a routine handover.
She's been afebrile with good pain control and is mobilizing well with physio; nothing acute has come up.
The one thing outstanding is her 20:00 anticoagulant dose, which hasn't been given yet — could your team make sure that happens?

clinical_knowledge.topic: Structured SBAR signout for a stable, low-concern post-operative patient at shift change
clinical_knowledge.review_status: grounded in AHRQ TeamSTEPPS SBAR principles and Joint Commission hand-off communication standards; local signout tools apply
core_concepts: Most shift handovers describe a stable patient, but the structure still matters: it prevents outstanding tasks from being lost between teams.
A routine signout should still explicitly state the one thing the receiving team must do, not just describe that the patient is fine.
diagnostic_clues: Stable vitals, controlled pain, and a clean wound support a low-concern signout, but an unadministered scheduled medication is still an active task to hand over.
common_misconceptions: A stable patient does not need a structured handover, only a brief mention.
Saying 'nothing to worry about' is a complete signout even when a scheduled task is still outstanding.
dangerous_errors: Omitting a scheduled medication or task from the handover because the patient otherwise seems uneventful.
Giving an unstructured, rushed signout that the receiving team cannot act on if something changes overnight.
management_principles: Use SBAR even for routine, low-concern patients so outstanding tasks are never lost at shift change.
Explicitly separate 'stable, no action needed' patients from 'stable, but one task outstanding' patients.
boundaries_and_exceptions: The exact format and content of a signout (verbal, written, or electronic) depend on local handover tools and ward policy.

source_refs.title: The Joint Commission: Hand-off Communications Standards
